subject: Biology
title: Mangroves: Trees in the Sea
description: Learn Mangroves: Trees in the Sea in one minute.

hook.text: Mangroves are trees that grow in saltwater—an environment that would kill most other plants.

buildup.text: Their tangled root systems rise above water, anchoring shorelines and sheltering young fish.

discovery.text: Mangroves filter salt through their roots and excrete it through their leaves.

twist.text: Mangrove forests store up to four times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests.

climax.text: They protect coastlines from storms and tsunamis—natural barriers worth billions in damage prevention.

punchline.text: Trees that drink saltwater and guard the coast.

quiz.question: How do mangroves handle salt?
options: They filter it through roots and excrete it through leaves
They only grow in low-salt areas

details.summary: Mangroves are trees adapted to grow in salty coastal waters, forming dense forests along tropical shorelines. Their aerial root systems stabilize coastlines, filter pollutants, and provide sheltered nurseries for fish and crustaceans essential to coastal fisheries and biodiversity.
details.whyItMatters: Mangroves protect coastlines from storms, tsunamis, and erosion while storing up to four times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests. Their rapid destruction for aquaculture and development leaves coasts dangerously exposed.
takeaways: Mangrove roots filter salt and stabilize shorelines against erosion and storms
They store four times more carbon per hectare than tropical rainforests
Over 35 percent of the world's mangrove forests have been lost since 1980

faq.question: How do mangroves survive in saltwater?
faq.answer: Different species use different strategies. Some filter salt out at the roots. Others excrete salt through specialized leaf glands. Some tolerate high internal salt concentrations. Their waxy leaves reduce water loss, and aerial roots allow gas exchange in waterlogged soil.

faq.question: Why are mangroves being destroyed?
faq.answer: Shrimp farming is the leading cause, converting mangrove forests to aquaculture ponds. Coastal development, agriculture, and logging also contribute. This removal leaves coasts vulnerable to storms, eliminates fish nurseries, and releases stored carbon, worsening climate change.
